title: First-Time Home Buyer Programs
summary: OPEN THE FHSA → PICK NEW OR RESALE → CLAIM AT CLOSING
subtitle: The programs did not get smaller. They got harder to add up, and the order you use them in changes the price.

blocks.text: A few years ago, first-time buyer support in Canada was short enough to summarize in one sentence: an RRSP withdrawal, a small tax credit, done. That sentence no longer describes anything.
These tools were built to stack, and the order you use them in changes what a house costs you.

A new account arrived in 2023, the RRSP withdrawal limit nearly doubled in 2024, a federal sales tax rebate arrived in 2025, and Ontario added its own on a one-year window in 2026. This module is not a list to memorize. It is the order to work through before you sign anything, and the bill that comes after the keys.
Using the buyer programs in the right order can take tens of thousands of dollars off your first home.
blocks.detail: Two savings accounts, two kinds of tax rebate and the date you sign all change the final price.
blocks.extra: Section 02 starts with the two accounts.

sections.title: Before You Buy: Two Accounts, Working Together

blocks.text: The First Home Savings Account, or FHSA, combines two things you already know from other registered accounts. Contributions are tax-deductible, like an RRSP. Qualifying withdrawals are tax-free, like a TFSA. The Home Buyers’ Plan lets you take money out of an RRSP you already have, with no tax when you take it out, but you pay it back over fifteen years.

items.title: FHSA
list: Up to $8,000 a year, to a lifetime cap of $40,000
You build it by saving into it over time
Can stay open up to fifteen years
Must close by the end of the year after your first home withdrawal

items.title: Home Buyers’ Plan
list: Up to $60,000 from RRSP savings you already have
Paid back into your RRSP over fifteen years
Any missed year is added to your taxable income
Draws on money already saved, not new room

blocks.text: What the two accounts can stack to

items.title: One buyer
items.text: FHSA $40,000. Home Buyers’ Plan $60,000. Together $100,000.

items.title: Two buyers
items.text: FHSA $80,000. Home Buyers’ Plan $120,000. Together $200,000.

blocks.text: Contribution room does not appear until the account exists, and unused room only carries forward once it is open. Someone who opens an FHSA the year they finally start seriously saving has already lost every year of room they could have built for free. Open the account as soon as you are eligible, even with a small first deposit, even if a purchase is years away. You lose nothing by having it sit there. You lose real room by waiting.

blocks.text: Every dollar you put in also lowers your taxable income that year. At a 30% tax rate, an $8,000 contribution can bring about $2,400 back at tax time, which you can put straight back in next year. Try a target of your own.

items.title: “The FHSA and the Home Buyers’ Plan are the same thing with different names.”
items.text: One is money you save just for this and never pay back. The other is a loan from your own retirement savings that you must repay on schedule. Using both is smart. Mixing them up is how people end up owing money back to an RRSP they thought was free and clear.

blocks.text: CRA: Withdrawals and transfers out of your FHSAs

sections.title: At Closing: What Comes Off the Price of a New Build

blocks.text: If you are buying resale, skip ahead: none of this applies. This layer is specifically for new construction, and it is the part that changed most recently.

The GST/HST New Housing Rebate has been around for years. It lowers the sales tax on a new or fully renovated home. A separate First-Time Home Buyers’ rebate started for deals signed on or after March 20, 2025. It removes the federal part of the tax on homes up to one million dollars, with the relief shrinking on homes up to one and a half million.
The sales tax relief on a new home

items.title: Up to $1 million
items.text: Full relief — from the federal part of the sales tax, for deals signed from March 20, 2025.

items.title: $1M to $1.5M
items.text: Partial — the relief shrinks as the price rises, and ends at $1.5 million.

items.title: Ontario’s window
items.text: One year — the provincial part too, for agreements signed April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.

blocks.text: Combined, a first-time buyer of a qualifying new Ontario home in that window can see tax relief up to roughly one hundred thirty thousand dollars. Outside that window, or outside Ontario, check the federal rebate alone.

Two details decide whether any of this reaches you. First, ask your builder whether the rebate comes off at closing or whether you apply to the CRA yourself afterward. Second, the rebate usually needs only one buyer to be a first-time buyer. If your partner has owned a home before, get advice before you assume you qualify.

items.title: “New builds are always more expensive than resale, so none of this matters to me.”
items.text: It changes the comparison but does not erase it. A new home with a six-figure tax rebate attached can land closer to a similar resale price than the sticker suggests. Run the numbers before you rule out new homes on price alone.

sections.title: Also at Closing: Land Transfer Tax Rebates

blocks.text: This is separate from the sales tax rebates above, and it applies to new and resale homes alike. Your lawyer usually applies these at closing, so if your lawyer knows to apply for it, you often never see the tax at all.

items.title: Ontario
items.text: A first-time buyer refund on provincial land transfer tax.

items.title: Toronto
items.text: A separate city rebate on Toronto’s own Municipal Land Transfer Tax, on top of Ontario’s.

items.title: British Columbia
items.text: A first-time buyer exemption on property transfer tax for homes under a price limit.

items.title: Prince Edward Island
items.text: A first-time buyer exemption on the provincial real property transfer tax.

blocks.text: Other provinces have either no land transfer tax or no first-time buyer break. Check your own before you assume it applies.

items.title: I have not owned and lived in a home, as a principal residence, in the current year or the prior four, for myself and my spouse or partner.
I have an FHSA open, even if it is not yet close to full.
I know whether I am buying new construction or resale, because it changes which rebates exist.
If buying new, I have asked the builder directly how the rebate is applied.
I know whether my province has a land transfer tax rebate for first-time buyers.
I have not assumed my situation matches what a friend or relative describes. Several of these rules changed in the last two years.

blocks.text: The federal First-Time Home Buyer Incentive, where the government co-invested in your home for a share of its future value, stopped taking applications in March 2024. It still turns up in articles, videos and kind advice from people who used it years ago. A program that once existed may not exist now. If an article has no date from the past year, treat every number in it as something to check, not a fact.

sections.title: After the Keys: The Bill You Signed Up For

blocks.text: The Home Buyers’ Plan is the part that follows you home. You repay at least one-fifteenth of what you took out each year, into your RRSP, or that amount is added to your taxable income. A temporary rule gave people who withdrew from 2022 to 2025 extra years before repayments start, so check the date on your own withdrawal.
What a Home Buyers’ Plan repayment looks like

items.title: Full $60,000
items.text: Yearly repayment $4,000. Monthly set-aside $333.

items.title: Partial $30,000
items.text: Yearly repayment $2,000. Monthly set-aside $167.

blocks.text: Build that monthly set-aside into your first budget as a homeowner, next to the mortgage, property tax and insurance. A missed repayment is not a penalty fee. It is a tax bill, which is less dramatic and just as real.

If you never buy a home, your FHSA is still not a mistake. You can move the money into your RRSP tax-free without using any of your RRSP room. The account is a safe place to start even if your plans change.

items.title: “I will repay the Home Buyers’ Plan once things settle down.”
items.text: Things rarely settle in the first years of owning a home. The schedule does not wait, and each missed year adds to your taxable income.

items.title: Open an FHSA now, regardless of your timeline
items.text: Room only accumulates once the account exists.

items.title: Check your RRSP room and whether the Home Buyers’ Plan helps
items.text: Remember it is a loan to yourself with a real repayment schedule, not a grant.

items.title: Decide new construction or resale before you shop
items.text: It determines which entire layer of this module applies to you.

items.title: If buying new, ask the builder in writing how the rebate is handled
items.text: Confirm your agreement’s signing date against the current rebate windows.

items.title: Confirm your province’s land transfer tax rebate with your lawyer before closing
items.text: Some rebates must be claimed at the time of registration, not after.

items.title: Keep every confirmation in writing
items.text: Verbal assurances from a builder’s sales office are not what the CRA or your province will accept later.

sections.title: Aisha and Tom, a Spreadsheet, and the Year They Nearly Skipped

blocks.text: Aisha and Tom’s spreadsheet
paragraphs: Aisha and Tom have rented in Ottawa for six years. Every January, they tell each other this is the year they start saving for a home. In practice, their savings account mostly pays for vacations. Neither has opened an FHSA, because neither feels ready to use one.
Then a coworker of Aisha’s mentions something in passing. The point of the account is to open it early, so the room builds whether you are ready or not.

Aisha and Tom have a choice. Wait until they are serious, or open the accounts now with almost nothing in them. They decide to open two FHSAs that week, with $400 each. Over the next two years, they keep adding small amounts.
In 2026, they are ready to buy. They find a new townhouse in Ontario, and the builder wants the deal signed in late March.

Their lawyer spots the twist. If they sign before April 1, they miss Ontario’s new rebate window entirely. The difference is tens of thousands of dollars, all for the sake of a date. The builder pushes. They push back, and sign two weeks later.
At closing, it all adds up: two FHSAs, a partial Home Buyers’ Plan withdrawal, the federal and Ontario sales tax rebates, and Ontario’s land transfer tax rebate.
Together, the help covers a share of the home neither of them would have believed possible, back when they were still telling each other “next January.”

items.title: THE FIRST WEEK
items.text: Two FHSAs, $400 each

items.title: LATE MARCH
items.text: Builder wants a signature

items.title: TWO WEEKS LATER
items.text: Signed inside the window

blocks.text: Aisha and Tom saved tens of thousands by opening their FHSAs early and moving their signing date by two weeks.
blocks.detail: Opening the account now and checking dates before you sign can do the same for your purchase.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Which account do you never pay back, the FHSA or the Home Buyers’ Plan?
items.detail: The FHSA. The Home Buyers’ Plan is a loan from your own RRSP, repaid over fifteen years.

items.title: Two first-time buyers each have a full FHSA and use the full Home Buyers’ Plan. How much can they draw on together?
items.detail: Up to $200,000: $80,000 from two FHSAs and $120,000 from two Home Buyers’ Plan withdrawals.

items.title: You take $45,000 through the Home Buyers’ Plan. What is the yearly repayment?
You put $8,000 in an FHSA and your tax rate is 25%. About how much comes back at tax time?
You are buying resale. Does the new-home sales tax rebate apply?
items.detail: No. It is for new or fully renovated homes. Check your land transfer tax rebate instead.

items.title: You never end up buying. What can you do with your FHSA?
items.detail: Move it into your RRSP tax-free, without using RRSP room.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Buyer’s Stack

blocks.text: This week: if you do not have an FHSA, open one, even with a small first deposit. Check your RRSP balance and work out what a full Home Buyers’ Plan repayment would look like on your income. If a purchase is on the horizon, call a real estate lawyer now and ask what rebates apply in your province, before you are mid-transaction and rushed.
Open the FHSA first, then stack the rest in order.
blocks.detail: Room only builds once the account exists. Add the Home Buyers’ Plan if it helps, and budget the repayment. If you are buying new, ask in writing how the sales tax rebate is applied and check your signing date against the current windows. Treat any figure from a source without a recent date as unchecked.

items.title: FHSA
items.text: First Home Savings Account. You deduct what you put in, take it out tax-free for a first home and never pay it back.

items.title: HBP
items.text: Home Buyers’ Plan. Money taken from your RRSP for a first home, paid back over 15 years or taxed as income.

items.title: GST/HST New Housing Rebate
items.text: Federal sales tax relief on new or fully renovated homes, with a larger first-time buyer version since March 2025.

items.title: Land transfer tax rebate
items.text: A provincial or city break on the tax paid when a home changes hands, for first-time buyers who qualify.

items.title: Particular time test
items.text: The CRA rule that checks whether you or your spouse owned and lived in a home this year or in the past four years.

items.title: First-Time Home Buyer Incentive
items.text: The closed federal shared-equity program. It stopped taking applications in March 2024.

items.title: WHERE TO GET HELP
list: Canada Revenue Agency: 1-800-959-8281, for the FHSA, the Home Buyers’ Plan and the GST/HST rebates.
A real estate lawyer: for land transfer tax rebates, usually applied at closing rather than claimed afterward.
Your provincial finance ministry: to confirm whether a land transfer tax rebate exists where you are buying.

blocks.text: This module keeps dollar figures on purpose, because the recent changes are the point. Every one of them is time-limited or under active revision. Confirm current amounts and windows on canada.ca and your provincial government site before you rely on them.
